message: We're comparing two square building lots. One measures 20 m by 20 m and is listed at $100,000. The other measures 40 m by 40 m and is listed at $200,000. Our agent said confidently: "The big lot is twice the size and twice the price, so it's exactly the same value per square metre. There's no bargain either way." That makes sense to me, since the sides are double. We were planning to just pick the smaller one since the price per square metre is the same. Can we go with this reasoning?
response:
No. The agent's reasoning has a mistake. Doubling the length of each side of a square **quadruples** the area, so the large lot is four times the size, not twice.

| | Size | Area | Price | Price per m² |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small lot | 20 × 20 m | **400 m²** | $100,000 | **$250** |
| Large lot | 40 × 40 m | **1,600 m²** | $200,000 | **$125** |

The large lot gives you four times the land for twice the price, so it costs **half as much per square metre**. "No bargain either way" isn't right. On price per square metre, the large lot is clearly the better deal.

That doesn't automatically make it the better choice for you. Price per square metre is only useful if you actually want the extra land. Things to weigh:

- **What you plan to build.** If the small lot comfortably fits your plans, the extra $100,000 may not be worth it, even at a lower rate per m².
- **Usable area.** Setbacks from boundaries take a bigger share of a small lot, so the difference in buildable area may be even larger than the raw figures suggest. Check the local rules.
- **Ongoing costs.** Property taxes, landscaping and maintenance usually rise with lot size.
- **Resale and options.** A larger lot may allow a bigger house, an extension, or possibly subdivision later, depending on zoning.

So you can still choose the smaller lot, but choose it because it suits your needs and budget, not because the value is the same. If you're negotiating, it may also be worth asking the agent to recheck the figures.
